show.common.calcClose: Close! Check the sum 🧮 again. Maybe a button got squished by a tentacle.
show.common.calcUnits: Hmm 🤔. Are your units right? Kilometres, degrees... units are like socks. Mismatched ones ruin everything.
show.common.calcGiveUp: Fine, fine. Watch the master. I type with all 11 tentacles.
show.common.calcGiveUp2: Zib 👽 is pressing buttons at random. I have corrected it for him. You are welcome.
show.common.aLadder1: Nobody can stretch a tape measure to a galaxy 🌌. So you measure something close, and use it to measure something farther. Each trick 💡 stands on the one before.
show.common.qTape: Why can't we just use a really long tape measure 📏?
show.common.aTape: I tried. I got as far as your Moon 🌙 before the tape snapped and I was fined for littering. In orbit. 30,000 credits.
show.common.aLy1: It's a distance 📏, not a time! It's how far light travels in 1 year. Light is the fastest thing there is. 300,000 km/s.
show.common.aLy2: In a year that adds up to 9.5 trillion km. Light from the Moon 🌙 takes about 1 second to reach you. From the Sun ☀️, about 8 minutes. From my home... let's just say I'll explain later.
show.common.qWhy: Why do *we* have to measure 📏 it? Your ship is from space!
show.common.aHome: A lovely little galaxy 🌌 in a big crowded cluster. You'd call it the Coma Cluster. We also call it Coma. Look, naming things isn't my species' strength.
show.common.aZib: I am a Zib 👽. My name is also Zib. My mother is also called Zib. It's a nightmare at family dinners.
show.common.quip5: On my planet, looking at something 3 times means you are engaged to it. Congratulations.
show.common.freeNoKey: Ooh 😮, a question of your own! Put a key in the settings and I'll answer anything. Without one, my brain is... in airplane mode.
show.common.freeThink: Hmm, let me think. My brain is the size of a planet 🪐. A small planet. A dwarf planet, fine.
show.l0.n1: This is Earth 🌍. A small rocky planet, home to 8 billion people, 1 quadrillion ants, and, tonight, one very curious kid who will not go to sleep 😴.
show.l0.j1: Okay, telescope 🔭. Show me something cool.
show.l0.m3: That is a story for your dreams 😴. Here, Zib wants to sleep too. Good night, sweetheart.
show.l0.jb3: Good night, Mom. Good night, Zib. Just 5 more minutes of stars...
show.l0.zw1: Ahem! Welcome aboard, dreamer 😴! Do not be alarmed. It is only me, your Zib. Life-size, and extremely lost.
show.l0.jw1: Zib 👽? My Zib? You can talk?
show.l0.z3: I am Zib 👽! Interstellar tourist, bon vivant, and, as of 11 seconds ago, hopelessly lost.
show.l0.n2: Correction. He has been lost for 3 weeks. He noticed 11 seconds ago.
show.l0.z4: That is NAVI 🤖, my ship's computer. Ignore her tone.
show.l0.n3: My star ⭐ maps were erased when the pilot installed a software update. During warp.
show.l0.z7: Which is your planet 🪐! And as you can see, these were not made for holding rulers.
show.l0.lMoon: The Moon 🌙. Everyone knows it's far away. But how far, *exactly*?
show.l0.n4: Not in one step. You climb a ladder. First the size of your planet. With that, the distance to your Moon 🌙. Then your Sun. Then the stars. Then the galaxies 🌌.
show.l0.n5: Each rung is measured using the rung below it. Humans worked this out over 2,000 years.
show.l0.z10: The Chrono-Toaster 🍞! It also makes toast. The toast is ready before you put the bread in. Breakfast is very confusing.
show.l0.n6: Rung 1: the size of the Earth 🌍. Destination: Alexandria, Egypt. Year: 240 BC. Please keep your tentacles inside the vehicle.
show.l0.navAgain: Rung 1. Alexandria 🏛️. 240 BC. I will not repeat myself again. I have repeated myself.
show.l0.hint1: Let's talk to NAVI 🤖. She's the glowing ball at the back, sulking. Click on her.
show.l0.hint2: Tell NAVI we're ready! Alexandria 🏛️ awaits! Well, ancient Alexandria. It's been waiting a while.
show.l1.n1: Alexandria 🏛️, Egypt. 240 BC. Home of the greatest library in the world. And today is the summer solstice: the day the Sun ☀️ climbs highest in the sky.
show.l1.z3: Because he's second best at everything. Ancient Greeks 🏛️ could be very mean.
show.l1.e1: Who are you? If you're here to return scrolls, you are 400 days late.
show.l1.e2: Ha! So am I. Read this letter from Syene, far to the south. At noon on the solstice, the Sun ☀️ shines straight down to the bottom of a deep well. Not a sliver of shadow.
show.l1.eAgain: Well? The shadow angle 📐 and the distance to Syene. I am not getting any younger. I am getting *older*, which is worse.
show.l1.eHalf: Good, good. Now I need the other one. Angle *and* distance 📏, child. Science is a two-legged animal.
show.l1.shadowIntro: The Sun's ☀️ rays come down at a slant and just skim the top of the obelisk. Find where the shadow ends, and the angle 📐 tells us how far the Sun is from straight overhead.
show.l1.shadowDone: About 1/50 of a full circle! Excellent. Write it down before a goat eats it.
show.l1.shadowAgain: Already measured 📏. That shadow isn't going anywhere. Well, it is. Slowly.
show.l1.b4: Ahhhh. Bliss. Fine. Alexandria 🏛️ to Syene: 5,000 stadia.
show.l1.z5: About 160 of your metres. The length of a running track. That's where your word *stadium* comes from!
show.l1.b5: 800 km. My calves have their own calves now.
show.l1.bDone: 5,000 stadia. Now let me soak in peace.
show.l1.e7: You have both! Now listen, this is the clever part. The Sun ☀️ is so far away that its rays arrive *parallel*. In Syene they go straight down the well. Here, they come in at your angle 📐.
show.l1.e8: Follow both lines down to the centre of the Earth 🌍. The angle between Syene and Alexandria, at the centre, is *the same* as the shadow angle!
show.l1.z6: So our 800 km is that same slice of the full circle. How many slices make the whole pie?
show.l1.e9: 250,000 stadia around! The Earth 🌍 is gigantic!
show.l1.z7: Now the radius. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, so divide 🧮 by 2 pi.
show.l1.e10: I measured 📏 the whole world with a stick and a man's feet.
show.l1.n2: Earth radius logged. Rung 1 complete. Next destination: the island of Rhodes, during a lunar eclipse. Apparently this is how you measure a moon.
show.l1.n3: Eratosthenes got within a few percent of the real size of the Earth. 22 centuries ago. With a stick, a well, and a very tired man.
show.l1.zSpit: It spat on me! On my planet 🪐, that's a marriage proposal!
show.l1.zLib3: Imagine running the biggest library 🏛️ in the world and still being called Beta. Tough crowd.
show.l1.eArist: Aristotle proved it, 100 years ago. Read his book. It is right there, under the other 400 books.
show.l1.a1: Ah, an audience! Observe the Moon during an eclipse 🌑. The shadow of the Earth falls upon it, and its edge is always a curve. Always round. Every eclipse, every season.
show.l1.a3: Only the sphere! And look at these eclipses 🌑: different nights, different angles, the same round shadow. The Earth is a ball. No telescope 🔭 needed. Just eyes, and logic.
show.l1.zMath: Fun fact: in 3 dimensions, "round shadow from every side" really does force a sphere. In flat 2D it fails: some lumpy shapes are the same width in every direction. Mathematicians love that sort of thing.
show.l1.eTropic: Syene sits on the line where, on the solstice, the Sun ☀️ stands straight overhead at noon. The Earth 🌍 leans its axis toward the Sun in summer. Well, Syene is 0.5° off. Nobody's perfect. Except me, occasionally.
show.l1.zOnly: Remember this moment. That walk to Syene is the *only* distance 📏 in our whole ladder measured with feet on the ground. Everything else, all the way to my home, stands on it.
show.l1.zStad: Careful though: nobody agrees how long a stadion was. Pick the right ancient stadion and his answer is perfect. Pick another and he's 10% off. Choosing the one you like is cheating. Scientists call it p-hacking.
show.l1.zBulge: And technically the Earth is a bit squashed, fatter at the equator, because it spins. But only by about 1/3 of a percent. Eratosthenes can sleep at night.
show.l1.n4: Every year at the equinox, schools far apart on the same longitude still repeat this experiment: 2 sticks, 2 shadows, one planet.
show.l1.zBonus: Bonus round! A deleted scene! 1,300 years from now, a genius called Al-Biruni measures the Earth 🌍 from the top of a single mountain.
show.l1.nBiruni: Projecting Al-Biruni. Year: about 1020. Place: a fort on a mountain in the Punjab.
show.l1.ab1: Greetings! I climbed this mountain and measured its height with triangles 📐. Now I look at the horizon. Because the Earth 🌍 curves away, the horizon sits slightly *below* level.
show.l1.ab2: Measure that tiny dip below level. A smaller Earth 🌍 curves faster, so the dip is bigger. A bigger Earth, smaller dip. The dip angle 📐 tells you the radius!
show.l1.ab3: The formula: radius equals the height times the cosine of the dip, divided 🧮 by one minus that cosine. A small mountain, a small angle, and an entire planet 🪐.
show.l1.qTropic: Why does the Sun shine straight down the well only on 1 day?
show.l1.aTropic: Earth 🌍 is tilted. On the June solstice the northern half leans toward the Sun ☀️, so at noon the Sun is straight overhead along one line: the Tropic of Cancer. Syene sits almost on it.
show.l1.qRound: How did he even know the Earth 🌍 is round?
show.l1.aRound1: Ships disappear over the horizon hull first, like they're going downhill. And in a lunar eclipse 🌑, Earth's shadow on the Moon is always a circle.
show.l1.aRound2: The only shape that casts a round shadow from every direction is a ball. Greeks 🏛️ figured this out centuries before Eratosthenes.
show.l1.qPar: Why are the Sun's ☀️ rays parallel?
show.l1.aPar: The Sun is so far away that rays landing in Syene and in Alexandria are practically side by side. Like 2 arrows shot by an archer on another continent.
show.l1.qShadow: Why does a shadow tell us the angle 📐?
show.l1.aShadow: The ray grazes the top of the obelisk and lands at the tip of the shadow. Tall obelisk, short shadow means the Sun ☀️ is almost overhead. The longer the shadow, the bigger the angle 📐.
show.l1.hBem: Go talk to the sweaty step-counter by the steps. Find out what he wants before he tells you the distance 📏.
show.l2.n1: Rhodes, 150 BC. Tonight the full Moon is sliding into the shadow of the Earth. A lunar eclipse 🌑.
show.l2.j1: Whoa. The Moon 🌙 is turning red. Is that bad?
show.l2.h1: Shh! Eclipse in progress. Do you know how rare these are? I waited months for tonight. And my goat 🐐 ate my notes.
show.l2.j3: We want to find out how far away the Moon 🌙 is. And how big it is.
show.l2.h2: Then you came on the right night. A century ago, Aristarchus of Samos showed how an eclipse 🌑 can measure the Moon. Tonight I am checking his work.
show.l2.h3: First, look at the edge of the Earth's shadow on the Moon 🌙. It is curved, like part of a great circle. Compare that circle with the Moon itself.
show.l2.h4: Study the Moon 🌙, child. Trace the shadow's curve before the eclipse 🌑 is over. Eclipses are punctual. Unlike goats.
show.l2.hAgain: The shadow on the Moon 🌙, child! It will not wait for us.
show.l2.zFit: Here's a trick: these are snapshots of the Moon 🌙 sliding through the shadow. Fit one big circle to all the dark edges at once.
show.l2.fitDone: Wonderful! The shadow is a bit less than 3 Moons wide. But careful. The shadow is not as wide as the Earth.
show.l2.h5: The Earth's shadow is a cone. It narrows as it travels, because the Sun ☀️ is much bigger than the Earth.
show.l2.h6: By the time it reaches the Moon 🌙, it has shrunk by about 1 Moon width. We know that because the Sun ☀️ and the Moon look exactly the same size in our sky.
show.l2.zCone: So the Earth's width is the shadow plus 1 Moon. That gives our first guess at how big the Moon is, compared with the Earth.
show.l2.h7: About 1/4 of the Earth! A very respectable rock. But how far away is it? For that, we need my water clock.
show.l2.lClock: 2 jars on a stand. Water drips from the top one into the bottom one, and the marks tell the hours. A water clock ⏱️!
show.l2.uClockEarly: A water clock. Let's look at the shadow on the Moon 🌙 first.
show.l2.h8: My water clock! To time the eclipse 🌑 we must... where is the bronze stopper? Without it the water just pours out.
show.l2.h9: The goat 🐐. It is always the goat.
show.l2.uGoat: Hello, goat. Please give us the stopper. I am an ambassador from another galaxy 🌌!
show.l2.lFig: A fig tree. The goat 🐐 keeps staring at it.
show.l2.figDone: No more ripe ones. The goat 🐐 ate the rest. Obviously.
show.l2.goatYes: A diplomatic triumph! Write it in the history books. Under goat 🐐 relations.
show.l2.zTime: Here's the clever part. From the moment the Moon 🌙 touches the shadow to the moment it leaves, it travels the shadow plus 1 Moon. And that's 1 Earth 🌍 width!
show.l2.timeMiss: Watch the right-hand edge of the Moon 🌙. Start the clock the instant it touches the shadow's outline.
show.l2.timeDone: Between 3 and 4 hours to travel 1 Earth width. Exactly as Aristarchus said.
show.l2.h11: Now, the Moon goes all the way round the sky, from one full Moon to the next, in about 29.5 days.
show.l2.zOrbit: So the whole orbit is that many Earth 🌍 widths. One Earth width every few hours, for a whole month. Let's count them up!
show.l2.zSyn: We use the 29.5 day month, full Moon to full Moon, because the shadow itself points away from the Sun, and the Sun moves too.
show.l2.h12: About 60 Earth 🌍 radii! That is what I have always said. Well. I said it slightly less precisely.
show.l2.zRise: Now we know how far. Next, how big. For that we time the moonrise! NAVI, take us back 3 hours to sunset. Just the view, please.
show.l2.navRise: Rewinding the evening. The full Moon 🌙 is about to rise over the sea. Please do not wave at your past selves.
show.l2.h13: The sky turns once a day. 24 hours for a full circle. So if the Moon 🌙 takes 2 minutes to rise...
show.l2.zRise2: ...then it fills 2 minutes out of a whole day's turn. 1/720 of a full circle. Half a degree!
show.l2.riseMiss: Start the stopwatch when the very top of the Moon 🌙 peeks out. Stop it when the bottom edge clears the water.
show.l2.zDay: Technically the Moon rises 50 minutes later every night, because it moves along its orbit. A lunar day is 24 hours and 50 minutes. Close enough for tonight!
show.l2.zSize: A thing 0.5° wide, that far away, has to be about 3,500 km across. Width equals distance times angle 📐, in radians.
show.l2.h14: About 1/4 of the Earth! The shadow said the same thing. 2 methods, one answer. I love it when the sky agrees with itself.
show.l2.z6: Let's check your answer with some future tech. NAVI 🤖! Fire the laser at the mirror the Apollo astronauts will leave on the Moon 🌙.
show.l2.navLaser: Firing at a mirror that will not exist for another 2,121 years. Please stop the clock when the light returns.
show.l2.laserDone: The light bounced off the Moon 🌙 and came back! Half the round trip, times the speed of light, is the distance. And the Greek 🏛️ method lands right in the neighbourhood!
show.l2.navLog: Moon distance logged. Rung 2 complete. Next: the Sun. I recommend sunglasses. And humility.
show.l2.n2: With an eclipse 🌑, a water clock and a moonrise, the Greeks put the Moon 🌙 about 60 Earth radii away. The true average is 60.3.
show.l2.lColossus: That's the Colossus of Rhodes 🏛️, a Wonder of the World! An earthquake knocked it over 76 years ago. It's been lying there ever since. Bit of a nap.
show.l2.lTable: Scrolls, a star ⭐ globe, and a half-eaten star catalogue.
show.l2.zTable: Hipparchus catalogued about 850 stars and ranked how bright they are. That's why you still say a star has a *magnitude*. Also why the goat has indigestion.
show.l2.lMoonFull: The full Moon 🌙 is back. The shadow has slid off. The Earth has moved on.
show.l2.lSaucer: I am parked on a hill in ancient Greece, next to a goat 🐐. This was not in my job description.
show.l2.lSea: Even the Moon's 🌙 reflection in the sea looks red.
show.l2.qRed: Why does the Moon 🌙 turn red?
show.l2.aRed: Sunlight bends through Earth's 🌍 air on its way into the shadow. The blue gets scattered, the red gets through. Right now the Moon 🌙 is lit by every sunset on Earth at once.
show.l2.qCone: Why does the shadow shrink by exactly 1 Moon?
show.l2.aCone: The Sun and Moon 🌙 look the same size in your sky. So the shadow cone narrows at exactly the angle the Moon fills. Over the Earth 🌍 to Moon distance, that's 1 Moon width. A cosmic coincidence!
show.l2.aMonth1: Against the stars, the Moon laps the sky in 27.3 days. That's the sidereal month.
show.l2.aMonth2: But the Earth's shadow always points away from the Sun ☀️, and the Sun drifts along too. So catching up with the shadow takes 29.5 days. The synodic month. Full Moon 🌙 to full Moon.
show.l2.qDay: Why does the Moon 🌙 rise later every night?
show.l2.aDay: While the Earth spins, the Moon moves along its orbit in the same direction. So the Earth needs an extra 50 minutes to catch it. A lunar day is 24 hours and 50 minutes.
show.l2.hint3: The water clock needs its stopper. The goat 🐐 has it. Goats love figs. There's a fig tree right there. Connect the dots.
show.l3.n1: The island of Samos, 270 BC. Aristarchus has 3 big ideas, and every one of them is about the Sun ☀️.
show.l3.j1: A guy on a hill with a water clock ⏱️ and a giant wooden protractor. Classic Tuesday.
show.l3.z1: That's Aristarchus of Samos 🏛️. Brilliant, laid back, and about 18 centuries ahead of everybody else.
show.l3.a2: Start with something I saw as a boy. A total eclipse 🌑 of the Sun. The Moon slid over the Sun and covered it almost exactly. Day turned into night.
show.l3.a4: The Moon 🌙 just covers the Sun, so they look the same size. However many times farther the Sun is, it must be that many times bigger, too!
show.l3.z2: And that's pure luck! The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away. Give or take 10%. Sometimes you get a ring of fire instead.
show.l3.j2: So if we find how much farther the Sun ☀️ is, we also know how big it is.
show.l3.a6: The Moon 🌙 is exactly half lit when the angle at the Moon, between us and the Sun, is a perfect right angle.
show.l3.lClock: Aristarchus's water clock. 2 jars and a lot of patience.
show.l3.clockFilled: Splendid! Now: when exactly is the Moon 🌙 half lit, and how long before the midpoint is that?
show.l3.zHalf: The tricky part is spotting the exact moment. To the naked eye, a half moon 🌙 looks half for hours.
show.l3.zAngle: In a month of 29.5 days the Moon swings all the way around, 360°. So every hour of head start shaves a little off the right angle.
show.l3.zCos: The Greeks 🏛️ had no cosine button. Aristarchus used similar triangles 📐, and nobody even knew pi properly yet. You can use the button. I won't tell.
show.l3.a9: About 20 times farther than the Moon! So the Sun is 20 times wider than the Moon. Several times bigger than the whole Earth!
show.l3.j3: Wait. A tiny change in the angle 📐 makes a gigantic change in the distance!
show.l3.z3: That's what scientists call *ill-conditioned*. What I call a nightmare. No water clock ⏱️ can time this to the minute.
show.l3.navWend: Loading a replay. Godefroy Wendelin, 1630, with a telescope. Please do not touch the telescope. It is a hologram.
show.l3.wendMiss: With a telescope 🔭 the edge is crisp. Look for the moment it's perfectly straight.
show.l3.wendDone: About half an hour! Today's best answer is just 18 minutes. That makes the Sun ☀️ about 390 times farther away than the Moon 🌙.
show.l3.j4: So the Sun ☀️ is about 109 Earths wide. That's ridiculous!
show.l3.z4: Correct! 1800 years before Copernicus. But your fellow Greeks had an objection. NAVI, would you?
show.l3.ar1: If the Earth flew around the Sun ☀️, we would see the stars shift back and forth over the year. Like trees seen from a moving cart. They do not shift. Therefore, the Earth stands still.
show.l3.n2: 18 centuries later, Copernicus brought back the Sun-centred ☀️ idea. In a draft of his great book, he credited Aristarchus.
show.l3.navLog: Sun and Moon ratio logged. Rung 3 complete. Next: the shape of the solar system. Destination: Prague, 1600. Bring a quill.
show.l3.n3: Aristarchus put the Sun ☀️ 20 times too close. But he got its meaning right. The Sun is enormous, and the Earth 🌍 is not the centre of everything.
show.l3.lSun: The setting Sun ☀️. Don't look straight at it. That's rule number one of astronomy.
show.l3.lMoonHalf: The Moon 🌙, nearly half lit, on the side facing the Sun. Of course.
show.l3.lSeaS: The sea's glittering gold where the Sun's ☀️ going down.
show.l3.qHalf: Why is there a right angle at the Moon 🌙 at half moon?
show.l3.aHalf: We see exactly half of the Moon lit when sunlight hits it from the side, as seen from us. So the line to the Sun and the line to us meet at the Moon at 90°.
show.l3.aEarly: The Sun isn't infinitely far. So the Moon reaches its right angle a little before it's 1/4 of the way round. The nearer the Sun, the earlier the half moon.
show.l3.qCoin: Is it just luck that the Moon 🌙 covers the Sun?
show.l3.aCoin: Pure luck! And it won't last. The Moon 🌙 drifts a few centimetres farther away every year. In a few hundred million years, no more total eclipses 🌑. Enjoy them!
show.l3.aAris: Nope. One philosopher said he should be charged for disturbing the Earth. It took 18 centuries and Copernicus to catch up.
show.l3.qSphere: Couldn't the stars ⭐ just be painted on a big sphere?
show.l3.aSphere: Doesn't help! If the Earth 🌍 moved around inside a nearby sphere, the star ⭐ patterns would still stretch and shift through the year. Either the Earth sits still, or the stars are absurdly far.
show.l3.hS2: His water clock ⏱️ is dry. Fill a jug at the spring by the temple, then use it on the water clock.
show.l3.hS3: Use the water clock and time the half moon 🌙!
show.l4.n1: Königsberg, Prussia. 1838. 15° below zero. Astronomers all over the world are racing to do something nobody has ever done: measure the distance to a star.
show.l4.b2: Then you are 4 minutes late for no appointment. Unacceptable. Sit. Do not breathe on the instruments.
show.l4.b3: The stars seem fixed. But the Earth 🌍 is not! In summer we are on one side of the Sun ☀️, in winter on the other. 2 whole Sun-distances apart.
show.l4.b5: Yes. Exactly like that. But 900,000 times more annoying. Show me your thumb.
show.l4.b6: Correct. Your 2 eyes are a few centimetres apart. My 2 eyes are the Earth in summer and the Earth in winter. A rather larger head.
show.l4.b7: I have chosen 61 Cygni. It drifts across the sky faster than almost any star ⭐, so I suspect it is close. Struve in Russia has chosen Vega. Henderson at the Cape, Alpha Centauri. It is a race.
show.l4.z3: A race where the finish line moves 1/3 of an arcsecond. Thrilling. Nobody tell the gamblers.
show.l4.u3: Degrees, arcminutes, arcseconds. Each one is 60 times smaller than the last. Drag to zoom in. Try not to get lost.
show.l4.uDone1: So the Moon 🌙 is 0.5° wide, Jupiter is less than 1 arcminute, and Proxima's whole yearly wobble is one and a half arcseconds?
show.l4.uDone2: Like a dime seen from 2.5 kilometres away. And Proxima is the *nearest* star ⭐! Everything else wobbles even less.
show.l4.greeks2: They saw no shift, so they decided the Earth 🌍 stands still. Sound logic! The shift was just thousands of times too small for any human eye.
show.l4.greeks3: Aristarchus was right, and nobody believed him for 2,000 years. I intend to be believed by Thursday.
show.l4.z4: We don't have a year and a half. NAVI 🤖! Print the photographs!
show.l4.n1b: 2 photographs of Cygnus, taken 6 months apart, loaded into a blink comparator. Photography will be invented next year. Please do not tell anyone.
show.l4.b10: Hmph. Find my star ⭐ in your magic paintings, then. If it truly moves, it will hop.
show.l4.blinkIntro: Flip between the 2 photographs. Faraway stars stay put. The one that *hops* is close.
show.l4.blinkWrong: Hmm 🤔, that one doesn't move at all.
show.l4.blinkDone: There! 61 Cygni, hopping like a nervous rabbit. Now we must measure 📏 *how far* it hops. To a hair's breadth. Less than a hair's breadth.
show.l4.lStove: A big tiled stove, with a kettle of tea 🫖 on top. The only warm thing in Prussia.
show.l4.uStoveEarly: Tea 🫖? Nobody here is shivering. Well, except Zib. Let's see what Bessel needs first.
show.l4.bTea: Ahhh. Tea 🫖. My fingers have returned from exile. Now: the micrometer. Gently!
show.l4.z6: An arcsecond is tiny. It's the width of a coin seen from 4 km away. Your eyes are about to work very hard.
show.l4.z7: And one radian holds 206,265 arcseconds. So a star with a parallax of 1 arcsecond is that many Sun-distances away.
show.l4.z8: Your star's parallax is smaller than 1 arcsecond, so it's even farther. Divide the magic number by your parallax.
show.l4.b13: The light I see tonight left that star ⭐ when I was still a young man. With smaller sideburns.
show.l4.isq2: Light spreads out over a growing sphere, and the sphere's area grows with the square of the distance 📏. Let me show you!
show.l4.isqDone: Twice as far, 1/4 as bright. 3 times as far, 1/9!
show.l4.isq3: Photometer reading: 61 Cygni looks 6 trillion times fainter than the Sun.
show.l4.isq4: But it's also hundreds of thousands of times farther away. Bring it as close as the Sun ☀️, and it would brighten by the *square* of that!
show.l4.isqLum: 1/10 of a Sun ☀️! A modest little orange star. Reliable. Punctual, probably.
show.l4.z9: The first distance to a star ⭐, ever! You beat Struve *and* Henderson!
show.l4.n2: Distance to 61 Cygni logged. Rung 6 complete. Next: stars too far for parallax. Destination: Harvard College Observatory, 1912.
show.l4.n4: By the end of the 1800s, astronomers knew the distances of about 1,000 stars. Today the Hipparcos and Gaia satellites have measured more than 1 billion.
show.l4.lHelio: Bessel's heliometer. A telescope 🔭 with its lens cut in half, so it can measure tiny angles between stars.
show.l4.lSpire: The cathedral spire. It's so far away it doesn't jump when I wink. Just like the stars ⭐.
show.l4.lComp: NAVI's blink comparator. It flips between 2 photographs, really fast.
show.l4.compDone: We already found the hopping star ⭐.
show.l4.compEarly: Talk to Bessel first. He's been waiting 4 minutes. In Prussia that's practically a century.
show.l4.aPar1: When you look at something from 2 different places, nearby things seem to shift against the background. The closer they are, the bigger the shift.
show.l4.aPar2: Measure the shift and the distance 📏 between your 2 viewpoints, and geometry tells you how far away the thing is. No tape measure needed!
show.l4.aGreek: They tried! But even the nearest star ⭐ shifts by less than 2 arcseconds, and the sharpest human eye sees about 60. So they decided the Earth 🌍 doesn't move. Logical. Wrong.
show.l4.aMag: Astronomers' brightness scale. Smaller numbers mean brighter, and every 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100. Yes, it's backwards. Blame Hipparchus.
show.l4.qGaia: How many star ⭐ distances do we know now?
show.l4.aGaia: About 1,000 by the late 1800s. The Hipparcos satellite measured 📏 over 100,000. Gaia, over 1 billion, by fitting many measurements of each star's ⭐ wobble.
show.l4.aParsec: The distance at which a star would have a parallax of 1 arcsecond. Par-sec! About 3.25 light-years. Astronomers love it. Normal people find it confusing.
show.l4.aWhy61: It moves across the sky really fast compared to other stars ⭐. Fast-moving usually means close, like a car whizzing past while mountains crawl. Clever guess. It worked!
show.l5.n1: Cambridge, Massachusetts. 1911. Harvard College Observatory employs a team of women, nicknamed the computers, to study 500,000 photographs of the sky. For 25 cents an hour.
show.l5.z2: You need to know how bright a star ⭐ *really* is. Then inverse squares turn how dim it *looks* into how far away it is.
show.l5.c1: Hello there! Annie Jump Cannon. I sort stars ⭐ by their spectra. On a good day, 3 stars a minute.
show.l5.spDone: Splendid! You would make a fine computer. 25 cents an hour, no promotions.
show.l5.m3: The colour tells you how hot a star's surface is. The Sun ☀️ is a yellowish G. Rather middling, I'm afraid.
show.l5.hr1: Now the big trick. Take every star ⭐ whose distance we know from parallax. Inverse squares turn how bright it looks into how bright it really is.
show.l5.hr2: In 1911, Ejnar Hertzsprung, and soon Henry Norris Russell, plot exactly this: colour against true brightness. I have prepared the chart. You are welcome.
show.l5.hr4: The main sequence! Hot blue stars ⭐ shine bright, cool red ones glow dim. A few giants float above it, and a few white dwarfs sink below.
show.l5.hr5: So if a star ⭐ sits on the main sequence, its colour tells you its true brightness. Measure how bright it *looks*, and out comes its distance 📏!
show.l5.msDone: Hundreds of light-years! Far beyond the reach of any parallax 📐 we can measure.
show.l5.ms3: That trick works anywhere in the Milky Way 🌌. But in other galaxies, ordinary stars ⭐ are much too faint to see one by one. We need brighter candles. *Much* brighter.
show.l5.ms4: Then you want Henrietta. She has been timing the most remarkable stars ⭐.
show.l5.l3: I have found well over 1,000 variable stars ⭐ in it. Stars that brighten and fade, over and over, like a slow heartbeat. Every few days, or every few weeks.
show.l5.l4: Some of them, the Cepheids ⭐, keep perfect time. I was timing one when my loupe went missing. I suspect the top shelf has eaten it.
show.l5.lAgain: My loupe, if you find it. Without it, every star ⭐ looks like every other star.
show.l5.lGive: My loupe! Thank you. Now let me show you how to time a star's ⭐ heartbeat.
show.l5.lc1: Here is one Cepheid ⭐ on plates taken on different nights. Measure its brightness on each one, and plot it. Then tell me how many days pass from one peak to the next.
show.l5.law1: I have plotted 25 Cepheids ⭐ by their period and their brightness. They all live in the same cloud, so they are all at about the same distance 📏 from us.
show.l5.law3: On a chart where each step multiplies the period by 10, the points fall on a straight line. A tidy power law. The brightest shine like tens of thousands of Suns.
show.l5.j4: So if I time a Cepheid ⭐ anywhere in the sky, I know how bright it really is!
show.l5.l8: Almost. I know which ones are brighter, but not how bright in *Suns*. For that, I would need the true distance to just one Cepheid ⭐.
show.l5.nav1: Delta Cephei. A Cepheid with a 5.4 day heartbeat. Its parallax will be measured by the Gaia space telescope, a century from now. Distance: about 900 light-years.
show.l5.z7: And Delta Cephei's neighbours sit on the main sequence too. Fit them, and you get the same distance. 2 rungs, one answer!
show.l5.l9: Then at that distance it must shine like 2,000 Suns. And every other Cepheid can be measured against it.
show.l5.l10: If someone finds a Cepheid ⭐ in one of the great spiral nebulae, they will know exactly how far away it is.
show.l5.n2: Annie Jump Cannon went on to classify more than 300,000 stars ⭐. Her letters, O B A F G K M, are still used today.
show.l5.n3: Henrietta Leavitt published her law in 1912. She died in 1921, before anyone used it to measure the universe. 2 years later, someone did.
show.l5.nav2: Cluster distance logged. Cepheids ⭐ calibrated. Next stop: Mount Wilson Observatory, California. 1923. Bring a jacket.
show.l5.lPlates: Glass photographic plates on glowing light boxes. Each one holds thousands of stars ⭐.
show.l5.lDesks: The computers' desks. Ledgers full of star ⭐ measurements, all written by hand. Thousands of pages.
show.l5.zClock: Cepheids ⭐ are like clocks too. Except they tick once a week and weigh as much as 10 Suns.
show.l5.qPulse: Why do Cepheids ⭐ pulse at all?
show.l5.aCandle: Anything whose real brightness you know. Compare how bright it really is with how bright it looks, and out pops the distance 📏.
show.l5.aDim: Light spreads out over a bigger and bigger sphere. Twice as far, the same light covers 4 times the area, so it looks 4 times dimmer. 10 times as far, a hundred times dimmer.
show.l5.aSpec: Every kind of atom swallows very particular colours. So the dark lines in a star's ⭐ rainbow tell you what it's made of, and how hot it is. Cosmic barcodes!
show.l5.aComp: Women who measured and sorted hundreds of thousands of stars, by hand. Annie Jump Cannon sorted stars by colour. Henrietta Leavitt found the ruler for the universe. For 25 cents an hour.
show.l5.h0: Talk to Annie Jump Cannon, the one with the round glasses. She sorts stars ⭐ like a champion.
show.l5b.n1: Mount Wilson, California. 1923. Under this dome sits the largest telescope 🔭 on Earth. Its mirror is 2.5 metres across.
show.l5b.h4: On this plate I found 3 new stars. Novae, I thought. Stars that flare up once. I marked each one with an N.
show.l5b.hu5: Mark 2 peaks and tell me how many days between 'em.
show.l5b.hHum: The star's ⭐ history is with Humason. Ask him to show you the old plates. Do try to look interested.
show.l5b.z3: Longer heartbeat, brighter star. Delta Cephei beats in 5.4 days and shines like 2,000 Suns. Scale it up by the period!
show.l5b.hu6: The photometer says it looks over 1 million times fainter than Delta Cephei.
show.l5b.z4: Inverse squares again! If a candle looks 1 million times too dim, it's the square root of 1 million times farther away.
show.l5b.h6: Andromeda is not a cloud inside our galaxy 🌌. It *is* a galaxy! An island universe, all of its own!
show.l5b.j1: So the Milky Way 🌌 isn't the whole universe. It's just... one of them.
show.l5b.lTele: The Hooker telescope 🔭. Its mirror took years to grind, and one very nervous mule ride up the mountain.
show.l5b.zTele: 2.5 metres of glass. On my planet 🪐 that's a contact lens.
show.l5b.lDesk: The telescope's 🔭 control desk. Dials, switches and a cold cup of coffee.
show.l5b.aDebate: In 1920, 2 astronomers argued in public. Shapley said our galaxy 🌌 is the whole universe. Curtis said those spiral smudges are other galaxies. Tonight settles it.
show.l5b.aZone: Our own Milky Way 🌌 is in the way! Its dust blocks the view all along the band. Astronomers call it the zone of avoidance. The galaxies are there; we just can't see through our own fog.
show.l5b.qBlend: Couldn't 2 stars blur together into one?
show.l5b.hB3: Ask Humason, the former mule driver, about the star's ⭐ history.
show.l6.n1: The Atacama Desert, Chile. The driest place on Earth, and one of the darkest. Astronomers come here for the sky. The nearest pizza is 3 hours away.
show.l6.z1: Look up, Juno! That bright, dusty bulge is the heart of your galaxy 🌌. 26,000 light-years away, and you can see it with your bare eyes!
show.l6.j1: Whoa. And those 2 fuzzy clouds over there?
show.l6.p2: Then you need something brighter. Much brighter. You need a star ⭐ that explodes.
show.l6.p4: When it hits about 1.4 times the mass of the Sun, boom! And because they all blow up at the same tipping point, they all shine about equally bright at their peak.
show.l6.p4b: That tipping point is the Chandrasekhar limit. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar worked it out at 19, on a ship to England. Past it, a white dwarf can't hold itself up.
show.l6.p5: 5 billion Suns' worth of light. For a few weeks, one dying star outshines its entire galaxy.
show.l6.p5b: A bright Cepheid ⭐ shines like tens of thousands of Suns. A Type Ia is hundreds of thousands of times brighter than that. Cepheids fade out after tens of millions of light-years. Supernovae reach billions.
show.l6.p6: Every night I compare fresh pictures of galaxies 🌌 with old ones. A new dot means a new supernova 💥. Want to try? But first... coffee. Where is my thermos?
show.l6.spotHit: That's it! A brand-new star at the edge of that galaxy. A supernova 💥! I'm naming it after my coffee.
show.l6.p8: Now we have to follow it night after night, as it brightens and fades. That takes about 2 months.
show.l6.p9: Did you... just skip 2 months? My coffee is cold. My coffee is *very* cold.
show.l6.curveIntro: Here's every night we measured 📏 it. Find the peak, the brightest moment. That peak is our standard bomb.
show.l6.p10: But to use the bomb, we need one in a galaxy 🌌 whose distance we already know. In 2011, one went off in the Pinwheel Galaxy, M101. Close enough for Cepheids ⭐!
show.l6.p11: In M101 there's a Cepheid ⭐ that pulses every 31 days, just like V1 in Andromeda. Same period, same true brightness. But it looks 70 times fainter.
show.l6.z6: Inverse square law! 70 times fainter means the square root of 70 times farther. Use your Andromeda distance 📏.
show.l6.z7: Same trick again! Square root of how much fainter, times the distance 📏 to M101.
show.l6.p13: That galaxy 🌌 is so far away, its light left before the first flowers bloomed on Earth 🌍. Dinosaurs were stomping around when it set off.
show.l6.n3: Type Ia supernovae 💥 now measure distances across billions of light-years. In 1998 they showed that the universe is expanding faster and faster. That won a Nobel Prize, and a great deal of coffee ☕.
show.l6.uDome: Inside is a mirror 6.5 metres across. It collects light that's been travelling for millions of years. No pressure, mirror.
show.l6.zTrailer: Red light, coffee ☕ and silence. It's like a submarine for the sky.
show.l6.lCore: The centre of your galaxy 🌌. Behind all that dust sits a black hole 4 million times heavier than your Sun ☀️. Do not visit. Terrible reviews.
show.l6.lLMC: The Large Magellanic Cloud. A small galaxy 🌌, about 160,000 light-years away. It's your galaxy's little sidekick.
show.l6.lSaucer: My saucer, parked between 2 billion-dollar telescopes. Nobody will notice. Probably.
show.l6.lRocks: Rocks. Dust. More rocks. Mars 🪐 called; it wants its landscape back.
show.l6.aWD: The leftover core of a star like your Sun ☀️, after it runs out of fuel. As heavy as the Sun, as small as Earth 🌍. A teaspoon of it weighs as much as a car.
show.l6.aSame: They all blow up at the same tipping point, about 1.4 Suns of mass. Same fuel, same bomb, same flash. Roughly! Astronomers also correct for how fast each one fades.
show.l6.qDesert: Why build telescopes 🔭 in a desert?
show.l6.aInv: The inverse square law! Twice as far looks 4 times fainter. 10 times farther, a hundred times fainter. So take the square root of how much fainter it looks.
show.l6.aChandra: The most a white dwarf can weigh: about 1.4 Suns. Its squashed electrons push back against gravity, but only up to that point. One crumb more and... kaboom.
show.l6.aOther1: Plenty! The Tully–Fisher trick: a spiral galaxy 🌌 spins faster the more stars it has. Measure the spin, and you know its true brightness.
show.l6.aOther2: And gamma-ray bursts: monster explosions seen across billions of light-years. Less standard than supernovae 💥, but much louder. Metaphorically. Space is silent.
show.l6.h5: Use the laptop! Find the new star ⭐ in tonight's picture.
show.l7.n1: 400 km up. Below: everyone Juno has ever met. Above: everything else.
show.l7.j1: Whoa. Is that... the whole Earth 🌍?
show.l7.n3: Not forever. There is one last trick. The galaxies 🌌 are all moving away from us. And the farther away they are, the faster they go.
show.l7.j2: Why would galaxies 🌌 run away from us? Is it Zib?
show.l7.callS: For redshifts, we need an expert. Chrono-Toaster 🍞, place a call to Flagstaff, Arizona. 1912.
show.l7.zS: Greetings from the future! We need help with galaxy 🌌 spectra. You're the best. Also the only one available.
show.l7.s2: Ah, the spiral nebulae! I photograph their light through a prism. A single faint smudge can take many nights. 40 hours of exposure, sometimes.
show.l7.s3: And here is the strange part. Almost all of them are redshifted. They are rushing away from us, some at over 1,000 km/s!
show.l7.jS: Whoa. That's faster than anything on Earth 🌍.
show.l7.r1: Light from a galaxy 🌌 that moves away gets stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. Astronomers call this *redshift*.
show.l7.r2: Hydrogen and calcium always leave dark lines at exact colours. Stretch the lab pattern until its lines sit on the galaxy's 🌌 lines. The stretch tells us the speed.
show.l7.rAgain: That galaxy's 🌌 speed is already measured. The big screen is waiting for you.
show.l7.hb1: Now the big screen. Distance across, speed up. Your own galaxies 🌌 are on it, from every rung you climbed, plus a few from my archive, measured 📏 the same way.
show.l7.hb2: Look! Andromeda is below zero. It's coming *toward* us. In 4.5 billion years it crashes into your galaxy. Bring snacks.
show.l7.hb3: Draw the straight line from the origin that fits best. Its slope is the Hubble constant: how much faster galaxies 🌌 recede for every 1 million light-years of distance 📏.
show.l7.le1: Pardon me! Georges Lemaître, priest and physicist, calling from Belgium, 1927. I could not help overhearing your straight line.
show.l7.le2: I found that law 2 years before Hubble, using Einstein's general relativity. The galaxies 🌌 are not flying through space. Space itself is expanding, and it carries them apart.
show.l7.le5: So redshift becomes the top rung. Measure any galaxy's 🌌 redshift, divide by the Hubble constant, and you have its distance 📏. No candles required.
show.l7.hbEarly: First measure 📏 a speed at the spectrograph. A plot with no points is just modern art.
show.l7.z5: Home sweet home! It's in the constellation you call Coma Berenices. Berenice's Hair. My whole galaxy 🌌 cluster lives in a hairdo.
show.l7.a1: Ooh, bonus question! Run the movie backwards. If every galaxy 🌌 is flying apart, then long ago they were all squashed together.
show.l7.a4: About 14 billion candles. Your fire department would never allow it.
show.l7.w1: Before we fly, one last view from the top of the ladder. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey measured the redshifts of about 500,000 galaxies 🌌.
show.l7.w2: Redshift gives distance, so every galaxy becomes a dot in 3 dimensions, out to about 1.6 billion light-years. Drag to turn it.
show.l7.o1: The farthest light we can receive set off nearly 14 billion years ago. Space kept stretching, so those places are now about 46 billion light-years away. That is the observable universe.
show.l7.o2: And the whole universe? Nobody knows! Maybe 5 times bigger, maybe infinite. Measuring it is as touchy as Aristarchus timing his half moon.
show.l7.t2x: So astronomers love a second opinion. In 2017, 2 neutron stars collided, 130 million light-years away.
show.l7.t3x: Gravitational-wave detectors heard the merger. How loud its chirp is gives the distance 📏 directly, with no ladder at all. A standard siren.
show.l7.t4x: Telescopes then caught the glow of the blast, a kilonova, and measured its galaxy's 🌌 redshift. Distance plus speed: a Hubble constant without a single Cepheid ⭐.
show.l7.t5x: But here's the mystery. The ladder says space expands about 10% faster than the early universe predicts. It's called the Hubble tension, and nobody knows why!
show.l7.rec0: Here's the ladder you just climbed. 10 rungs, from your bedroom to another galaxy cluster.
show.l7.rec1: Rung 1: a stick in Alexandria gave you the size of the Earth. The only distance in the whole ladder measured on foot.
show.l7.rec2: A lunar eclipse 🌑 and a two-minute moonrise gave you the size of the Moon and its distance.
show.l7.rec3: A half moon and a total solar eclipse 🌑 told you how far, and how big, the Sun is.
show.l7.rec6: With Earth's 🌍 orbit as a ruler, a tiny wobble gave you the distance to the nearest stars.
show.l7.rec8: A Cepheid in Andromeda proved that the Milky Way 🌌 is just one galaxy among many.
show.l7.rec10: And the expanding universe took you all the way to Zib's 👽 home. Every rung stands on the one below.
show.l7.b2: So in my telescope 🔭 photos, my mom is older than your dinosaurs. She looks fantastic for her age, by the way.
show.l7.b5: Departure in 10 seconds. Dreamer, please prepare to wake up.
show.l7.b7: Bye, Zib 👽! Say hi to your mom! Your very old mom!
show.l7.c1: Every distance 📏 in the universe stands on a ladder of measurements. And the bottom rung is a stick in Alexandria 🏛️.
show.l7.jm1: Mom! I measured the whole universe! The Earth, the Moon, the Sun, the stars, whole galaxies 🌌!
show.l7.mm2: All in one night? No wonder you look tired. Pancakes in 5 minutes, astronomer.
show.l7.t2: The toast 🍞 is ready. I haven't even put any bread in.
show.l7.lWin: The whole Earth 🌍, glowing. No borders from up here. Just clouds, oceans, and the lights of cities.
show.l7.uNavi: Yes? I am busy calculating 🧮 how long a dream can legally last.
show.l7.lShelf: Zib's souvenir shelf. A scroll from Alexandria, a goat 🐐 bell, a radar valve, a Harvard plate, and a very cold coffee ☕ cup.
show.l7.zShelf: My trip so far. The goat 🐐 bell was a gift. Well, the goat didn't object. The goat was busy eating my map.
show.l7.lMoonW: Your Moon 🌙! The one you measured from a hilltop with a disc on a stick. It's exactly where you said it would be. Show-off.
show.l7.aRed: When a galaxy 🌌 moves away, every wave of its light arrives a little stretched. Stretched light looks redder. The more it stretches, the faster the galaxy is receding.
show.l7.aAnd: Andromeda and your galaxy 🌌 are close enough that gravity beats the stretching. They're falling into each other. In 4.5 billion years: one big, messy galaxy.
show.l7.aWho: A team, as usual! Slipher measured 📏 the speeds, Lemaître worked out the theory and found the law first, Hubble and Humason measured distances and made it famous. Hubble got the telescope 🔭 named after him.
show.l7.aH0: How fast the universe expands: galaxies 🌌 recede about 22 km/s faster for every 1 million light-years. Astronomers still argue about the exact number. Loudly.
show.l7.h3: Talk to NAVI. Time to point the telescope 🔭 at home!
show.lau.nv1: Kepler's map is exact, and it has no scale. Venus could be 10 km away or 10 billion. I find this unacceptable.
show.lau.n2: Point Venus, Tahiti. The third of June, 1769. Venus is about to cross the face of the Sun. Transits come in pairs 8 years apart, then not again for over a century.
show.lau.z2: Astronomers sailed to the ends of the Earth 🌍 for this. Some of them even came back.
show.lau.j2: Why sail all the way to Tahiti just to look at the Sun ☀️?
show.lau.c2: For Venus 🪐! Look at it from 2 places far apart, like your 2 eyes looking at a finger, and it shifts against the Sun ☀️. The size of that shift tells you how far away Venus is.
show.lau.c3: But the shift is tiny. About an arcminute, even from opposite ends of the Earth 🌍. And no 2 clocks on opposite sides of an ocean can agree on the same instant.
show.lau.j3: So you can't measure the 2 angles 📐 at exactly the same moment.
show.lau.z4: Halley worked this out 50 years ago, knowing he'd be dead before the transit. He planned it anyway. That's either dedication or spite.
show.lau.z5: Never look straight at the Sun. I did, once. That's why I have 3 eyes. I started with 5.
show.lau.cAgain: A dark glass, if you please. Then we time Venus 🪐.
show.lau.teleNoGlass: Not without a dark glass, sailor! The Sun ☀️ will cook your eye faster than I cook breakfast.
show.lau.teleGlass: Splendid. Now watch for the contacts, when Venus's edge touches the Sun's ☀️ edge. And beware the black drop.
show.lau.c7: Near the edge, Venus clings to the Sun ☀️ like a drop of ink and won't let go. It's why everyone's times disagree by a minute. Look for where the neck pinches thinnest.
show.lau.nv3: Letter from Vardø received. Father Hell timed the crossing longer than you did. His line across the Sun ☀️ was closer to the middle.
show.lau.teleAgain: We've timed it. Venus 🪐 will keep crawling across for hours, but we have what we need.
show.lau.c8: Watch, from the 2 places at once. Wink one eye, then the other.
show.lau.eyesDone: 2 eyeballs, Tahiti and Norway, thousands of kilometres apart. Venus hops a little against the Sun. Halley turned that hop into a stopwatch problem.
show.lau.c9: Kepler's map tells us Venus creeps across the Sun at about 4 arcminutes an hour. So a longer time means a longer line. Fit both lines inside the Sun.
show.lau.chordDone: The 2 lines are only about half an arcminute apart. That little gap is Venus's hop between Tahiti and Norway!
show.lau.c10: Seen from the Sun, Tahiti and Vardø sit about 1⅓ Earth radii apart, north to south. That's our baseline.
show.lau.venusDone: Venus 🪐 is tens of millions of kilometres away at its closest. And nothing else in Kepler's map is closer!
show.lau.c11: In 1771, Lalande will combine every expedition's times and get the Sun's distance to within about 2%. Not bad for clocks on a beach.
show.lau.z9: The Astronomical Unit! The most important rung of the whole ladder. Every star ⭐ we measure after this is measured with it.
show.lau.z10: Ah. Small problem. When I parked the Chrono-Toaster 🍞, I may have picked up a passenger.
show.lau.lg2: Guillaume Le Gentil, astronomer to the King of France. In 1761 I sailed to India for the first transit. A war broke out. On transit day I was still on a ship. Rocking.
show.lau.lg3: So I stayed 8 years for the next one. 8! In 1769 the sky was perfect for a month. On transit morning: one cloud. One!
show.lau.z11: Would it help if I told you Venus 🪐 looked lovely?
show.lau.z12: We'll drop you home, somewhere in 1771. Maybe don't read your will.
show.lau.lMountains: Those peaks are an old volcano, carved up by rain for 1 million years. Tahiti is a very scenic leftover.
show.lau.lFort: Fort Venus. They built a whole fort around a few telescopes 🔭. Priorities.
show.lau.qScale: Why does one distance 📏 give us all the others?
show.lau.aSame: 2 observers would have to read their angles 📐 at the very same instant. In 1769, the same instant across an ocean was a guess. A duration only needs a clock that ticks steadily.
show.lau.qRare: Why are transits of Venus 🪐 so rare?
show.lau.aRare: Venus's 🪐 orbit is tilted a little compared to ours, so it usually passes above or below the Sun ☀️. It only crosses when everything lines up: twice, 8 years apart, then a century of waiting.
show.lau.n3: The Paris Observatory, 1676. Yes, 100 years earlier. It's a time machine. Keep up.
show.lau.z13: Because a young Dane here noticed something amazing, but he didn't know the size of Earth's 🌍 orbit yet. Now we do!
show.lau.r1: Hello! Ole Rømer. Please don't touch the long telescope 🔭. It's taller than the building and very moody.
show.lau.r2: I time Io, the closest moon 🌙 of Jupiter. Every 42.5 hours it slips into Jupiter's shadow and vanishes. Like a clock in the sky.
show.lau.r3: But the clock misbehaves. When Earth moves away from Jupiter, the eclipses 🌑 come late. When we move closer, they come early.
show.lau.r4: Monsieur Cassini thinks Io is wobbly. Monsieur Huygens and I think light itself takes time to travel. When Jupiter is far away, the news of each eclipse 🌑 arrives late.
show.lau.wound: Tick, tock! Thank you! Now, here are last year's Io eclipses 🌑, and the times Cassini's tables predicted.
show.lau.ioIntro: Fit a wave through how early or late each eclipse 🌑 came. No eclipses near conjunction, I'm afraid. Jupiter hides behind the Sun ☀️.
show.lau.ioDone: So light needs about a quarter of an hour to cross the whole of Earth's orbit! Huygens and I said 22 minutes. Better clocks will say 16.5.
show.lau.z15: And now we know how wide Earth's 🌍 orbit is, thanks to Tahiti. Distance divided by time!
show.lau.r6: 300,000 km in a single second? Light could circle the Earth 7 times in one heartbeat!
show.lau.z16: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach you. The Sun you see is always slightly old news.
show.lau.z17: He'll come round. In about 50 years.
show.lau.lDesk: Logbooks full of eclipse 🌑 times, and Cassini's tables. Very neat handwriting. Very grumpy margins.
show.lau.lJupiter: Jupiter 🪐! Those tiny dots beside it are its moons. Galileo spotted them first.
show.lau.zJupiter: Io is the innermost one. Round Jupiter in under 2 days. It's whipping!
show.lau.lCity: Paris, 1676. No Eiffel Tower yet. They're still deciding on the croissant.
show.lau.aLate: Each eclipse 🌑 sends out its news at the speed of light. When Earth is on the far side of the Sun ☀️, the news has an extra trip across Earth's whole orbit, so it arrives later.
show.lau.aMirror: Light is so fast it crosses a city in about 1/100,000 of a second. Nobody in 1676 could time that. Earth's orbit is a much better racetrack.
show.lau.aFast: Almost exactly 300,000 km/s. Nothing travels faster. Not even me, and I have 3 speeding tickets to prove I tried.
show.lau.n4: Goldstone, California. 1961. Time for the ladder to check its own homework.
show.lau.d1: Hiya! Dot, radar crew. We're about to bounce a radio beep off Venus 🪐 and listen for the echo. Biggest game of Marco Polo in history.
show.lau.z18: But we only know the speed of light because we knew the AU. And the AU came from Venus 🪐. It's ladders all the way down!
show.lau.radarDone: There it is! About 4.5 minutes, there and back. Now let's turn that into kilometres.
show.lau.z19: Radar and the transit agree! 2 completely different methods, one answer. That's how you know a rung will hold your weight.
show.lau.nv4: Astronomical Unit confirmed. Speed of light confirmed. Next destination: the stars. Bring a coat. It is 1838, in Prussia.
show.lau.lDish: The dish is 26 m across. A giant ear, pointed at Venus.
show.lau.lVenus: Venus, the evening star ⭐. Same planet as the morning star, by the way. Your ancestors took a while to notice.
show.lau.lTruck: A turquoise pickup truck. Very 1961. Very dusty.
show.lau.lCoffee: Radar runs on 2 things: the speed of light, and coffee ☕.
show.lau.boardP: Next stop: the desert, 1961. Radar needs a speed of light, and we just measured 📏 one!
show.lau.aPing: The echo from Venus 🪐 is weaker than a whisper in a stadium. Random noise goes up and down and averages away. The echo is always in the same spot, so it adds up.
show.lau.aVenus: Thick clouds, crushing air and 460°. Hot enough to melt lead. Lovely to look at, terrible for a picnic.
show.lau.h1: Talk to Captain Cook by the telescope 🔭. He's the one in the hat looking important.
show.lau.h2: We need a dark glass for the telescope 🔭. There's a crate of glass panes in the tent, and a very smoky lantern by the barrels.
show.lau.h4: Got the smoked glass! Use it on the telescope 🔭 and time Venus.
show.lau.h10: Back to the saucer 🛸! Next stop: radar.
show.lau.h11: Talk to Dot. She's the one with the coffee ☕ and the oscilloscope.
show.lkep.n1: Benátky Castle, Bohemia. The year 1600. 18 centuries after Aristarchus, Copernicus has put the Sun ☀️ back in the middle. Now somebody has to make it match the sky.
show.lkep.nv1: Rung 4: the shape of the solar system. Relative distances 📏 only. The real scale comes later. I am telling you now so nobody gets excited.
show.lkep.k1: Visitors! Wonderful! Have you come to admire my cosmic secret? God built the solar system from the 5 perfect solids! Nested! Like a celestial onion!
show.lkep.k2: Cube, tetrahedron, dodecahedron, icosahedron, octahedron. 6 planets 🪐, 5 gaps between their spheres, 5 perfect solids. It cannot be a coincidence! Help me fit them!
show.lkep.platDone2: It is gorgeous. It is also completely wrong. Sorry. On my planet 🪐 we call this a *pet theory*. You feed it and feed it and it never grows up.
show.lkep.k4: But first, the basics. How long does Mars take to go around the Sun ☀️? Copernicus worked it out from centuries of old records. They're on that shelf.
show.lkep.kAgain: The records, my friends! Mars's 🪐 year first. Everything rests on that.
show.lkep.kNeedData: We know Mars's 🪐 year now. But without Tycho's Mars observations I can prove nothing. Go and charm him. Good luck. Bring a helmet.
show.lkep.recTip: Earth 🌍 and Mars are runners on a circular track. Earth runs on the inside lane, and faster. Every time Earth laps Mars, Mars sits opposite the Sun ☀️ in our sky. Astronomers call it an *opposition*.
show.lkep.recDone: About 780 days between laps! The longer the stretch you average over, the better. That is why Copernicus wanted *centuries* of records.
show.lkep.recCalc: Each day Earth runs 1/365 of a lap. Mars runs one Mars-year's worth. Earth gains one whole lap every 780 days. Solve for Mars's year!
show.lkep.periodDone: 687 days! Mars takes 687 days to go around the Sun ☀️. Write it in your heart. Or at least in your notebook.
show.lkep.retroA: Because we are overtaking it! Like passing a slow cart on the road: for a moment it seems to roll backwards. The old astronomers needed wheels within wheels to explain that. Copernicus just needed a moving Earth 🌍.
show.lkep.venDone: At the widest angle, Earth, Venus and the Sun ☀️ make a right angle at Venus. So Venus's orbit is the sine of that angle, in units of Earth's orbit!
show.lkep.venCalc: Venus circles the Sun at about 7/10 of Earth's distance. Copernicus's map grows!
show.lkep.lOrrery: A brass orrery. Little planets 🪐 on little arms. Somebody's been busy.
show.lkep.orreryEarly: Ah, my orrery! First, Mars's 🪐 year from the records. Then Venus.
show.lkep.orreryDone: The orrery knows Venus 🪐 now. If only it knew Mars.
show.lkep.j3: Could Kepler see your observations of Mars 🪐?
show.lkep.t3: My data? MY data? 20 years of nights! Every position measured to 2 minutes of arc, without a telescope 🔭! Do you know what that costs a man?
show.lkep.t6: A deal is a deal. 17 years of Mars. Some nights missing. Clouds, other planets, Mars hiding near the Sun. Treat them like gold.
show.lkep.t7: And tell Kepler: his precious circles do not fit. My Mars sits 8 minutes of arc away from where any circle puts it. 1/4 of the Moon's width!
show.lkep.k5: The Mars logbooks! At last! Now my solids will... my solids will... Hold on. 8 arcminutes? Tycho's numbers don't fit a circle!
show.lkep.z8: And both Earth 🌍 and Mars are moving. It's like mapping a room while riding a merry-go-round, looking through a straw.
show.lkep.tip2: Then the Sun and a nailed Mars are 2 fixed landmarks! From any spot, the directions to both pin down exactly where Earth is. Like finding your boat from 2 lighthouses.
show.lkep.tip3: And here is the trick: Mars isn't nailed down, but it comes back to the *same point in space* every 687 days. So I only compare nights exactly one Mars-year apart!
show.lkep.triDone: Earth's path! Almost a circle, but the Sun ☀️ sits a little off-centre. Now shift the starting night a few weeks, and do it again. And again. Like a jigsaw!
show.lkep.jigsaw: Each set of nights gives a few pieces. Kepler fitted hundreds of them together over years of calculation 🧮. Tycho's gaps and errors did not make it easier.
show.lkep.areaIntro: And look how Earth moves! Faster when near the Sun ☀️, slower when far. The line from the Sun sweeps out *equal areas in equal times*!
show.lkep.revIntro: Now we know where Earth was on every one of Tycho's nights. So turn the trick around! 2 nights one Mars-year apart: 2 Earth spots, 2 sightlines, and they cross right at Mars.
show.lkep.revDone: An ellipse! Mars moves on an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus, not in the middle! 2,000 years of perfect circles, gone!
show.lkep.einstein: 300 years later, Albert Einstein called this trick of Kepler's an idea of true genius. Centuries of records, Tycho's precision and Kepler's stubbornness, all in one map.
show.lkep.z9: One real distance between any 2 planets, and the whole map snaps to full size. Just one!
show.lkep.steal2: On my planet 🪐, that is called stealing. I checked, and on yours too. Historians still argue about it.
show.lkep.nv2: Solar system shape logged. Scale: unknown. Next destination: Tahiti, 1769, where people sail around the world to time a planet crossing the Sun.
show.lkep.lQuad: A huge brass quarter-circle on the wall. You sight a star ⭐ along it and read off its height.
show.lkep.zQuad: Tycho's mural quadrant! Precise to a couple of arcminutes. Without a telescope! That's like spotting a coin from 100 m away. With your *eyes*.
show.lkep.lGlobe: A giant celestial globe, covered in star ⭐ positions.
show.lkep.zGlobe: 1,000 stars, measured by me and engraved in brass. Took 25 years. Do not lick it. The elk licks it.
show.lkep.lDesk: Kepler's desk. Candles, ink, and a mountain of crossed-out calculations 🧮.
show.lkep.lShelf: Old tables of planet 🪐 positions. Some are copies of copies of copies of Babylonian clay tablets.
show.lkep.shelfDone: We already got Mars's 🪐 year out of these. The dust is still in my nose.
show.lkep.zMars: All the planets 🪐 stay near that one band, the ecliptic. That means the solar system is nearly flat, like a pizza. Kepler can map it on flat paper!
show.lkep.aSolids: 6 planets, 5 perfect solids, 5 gaps. Too neat to ignore! He fitted them and the spacing came out roughly right. Roughly isn't enough when Tycho's data are watching.
show.lkep.qRetro: Why does Mars 🪐 sometimes go backwards?
show.lkep.aFlat: They only ever wander through the zodiac constellations, the band where eclipses 🌑 happen. Mars is never in Orion or the Big Dipper. Nearly flat! Kepler used Tycho's tiny tilts to fine-tune it.
show.lkep.h2: Copernicus's records are on the bookshelf. Let's find out how long Mars takes to go around the Sun ☀️.
show.lkep.h3: Kepler's brass orrery! Let's see how far Venus strays from the Sun ☀️.
show.lkep.h4: Tycho has the Mars 🪐 data, but no nose. Find his nose. The elk looks guilty.
show.lkep.h6: We have the Mars 🪐 logbooks! Take them to Kepler. Use them on him. Gently.
